source.version: Saved 216-page preprint marked "Preprint, under review" throughout. No arXiv version number or revision date is printed. The text refers to publication in June 2025 (pp. 151, 154), but reference 129 is dated December 4, 2025 and says retrieved December 12, 2025 (p. 166); the saved file cannot confidently be labeled as the original June version.
source.title_on_document: Your Brain on ChatGPT: Accumulation of Cognitive Debt when Using an AI Assistant for Essay Writing Task

supplement.where: Appendix A-BC, PDF pp. 167-216. The paper also gives https://www.brainonllm.com/ for more information (p. 5), but does not identify a separate external statistical supplement.
supplement.holds: Appendix A lists interview clusters. Appendices B-BC provide EEG connectivity figures and detailed dDTF sums, connection counts, significance markers, and electrode-pair values. They do not supply missing arm-level essay-rating or linguistic-diversity means/SDs/SEs.

paper_design_summary: In a laboratory essay-writing experiment, people were randomly assigned to ChatGPT, web search without AI, or no aid for three sessions; the reported analysis retains 54 people. An optional fourth session reused 18 of these participants, switching former ChatGPT users to no tools and former unaided writers to ChatGPT on a previously chosen topic. The essays received teacher and AI-judge ratings, including uniqueness and content quality, and computational similarity analyses; EEG and interviews measured separate process and memory outcomes.

studies.label: SAT-style essay writing across three assigned-tool sessions and an optional crossover follow-up

assignment.what_was_assigned: Individuals were randomly assigned to LLM, Search Engine, or Brain-only, balanced by age and gender, and kept that assignment for sessions 1-3 (p. 23). Session 4 was optional and switched tools according to original assignment; it was not a new randomization and no randomized condition order is reported (pp. 28, 45, 117).
assignment.quote: Participants were randomly assigned across the three following groups, balanced with respect to age and gender:
assignment.locator: p. 23, Experimental Design: Participants; pp. 28 and 117, session-4 protocol
assignment.prereg_locator: No preregistration identified in the full PDF; experimental design is on pp. 22-29.

arms.name: LLM / ChatGPT (sessions 1-3)
arms.description: ChatGPT was the sole permitted information resource; other websites and LLMs were prohibited, with an account provided by experimenters (pp. 23, 27). There are 18 analyzed participants per original group (p. 3, Table 1).

arms.name: Search Engine (sessions 1-3)
arms.description: Websites/search permitted; ChatGPT and other LLMs prohibited. All used Google, and queries had -ai added to avoid AI-enhanced answers (p. 23). Group count: p. 3, Table 1.

arms.name: Brain-only (sessions 1-3)
arms.description: No online or offline aids or LLMs; participants relied on their knowledge, using a typing application (pp. 23, 27-28). Group count: p. 3, Table 1.

arms.name: LLM-to-Brain (session 4; returning subset)
arms.description: Returning original LLM participants wrote without tools in session 4. This is a subset, not additional people or an independently randomized arm. Nine original LLM participants are identified in p. 46 denominators; transition: pp. 28, 117.

arms.name: Brain-to-LLM (session 4; returning subset)
arms.description: Returning original Brain-only participants used ChatGPT in session 4. This is a subset, not additional people or an independently randomized arm. Nine original Brain-only participants are identified in p. 46 denominators; transition: p. 117.

participants.exclusions: Methods state 60 recruited, 55 completing at least three sessions after scheduling difficulties, and data reported for 54 "To ensure data distribution" (p. 22). Randomized denominator, assignment-stage arm counts, and arm-specific losses are not stated. Session 4 was optional: 18 returned, with 9 from each original LLM and Brain-only group (pp. 45-46, 117); these people are already in the 54.
participants.who: Adults recruited from MIT, Wellesley, Harvard, Tufts, and Northeastern in greater Boston, mostly undergraduate/postgraduate students, with some university-employed graduates (postdoctoral researchers, research scientists, software engineers). Ages 18-39 (p. 22). Educational-status subtotals do not reconcile with the analyzed count; the explicit 54 is retained.
participants.country: United States (greater Boston recruitment, p. 22; country shown on p. 1).
participants.quote: To ensure data distribution, we are here only reporting data from 54 participants (as participants were assigned in three groups, see details below).
participants.locator: p. 22, Experimental Design: Participants; p. 3, Table 1; pp. 45-46 and 117, session-4 sample

ai_tool.name_model: OpenAI ChatGPT; the intervention model/version is not stated in the PDF.
ai_tool.how_used: Free-form interaction through a supplied account during essay production; requests could cover drafting, ideas, structure, revisions, translation, or information. Other resources were prohibited in the LLM condition (pp. 23, 27; pp. 65-68, Figures 28-33). The local llama4:17b-scout-16e-instruct-q4_K_M model is the researchers' analysis/judging tool, not the stated participant intervention.

task.description: Write an argumentative essay from a self-selected SAT prompt. Each of sessions 1-3 offered three prompts, for nine topic options. Session 4 offered only the three topics previously chosen by that participant, with tools switched and no advance notice (pp. 25-28). Teacher uniqueness ratings and cross-writer similarity analyses make the task relevant to the codebook.
task.duration: 20 minutes writing per session (p. 27); sessions 1-3 required, session 4 optional (pp. 23, 28). The study took place over four months, but individual intersession delays are not stated (p. 23).

outcomes.name: Essay uniqueness: English-teacher ratings with AI available
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Two English teachers, blinded to group assignments and study motivations, scored essays on a 0-5 scale (p. 72). Figures report averaged essay assessments and aggregations by topic, session, and group; no participant-level standard errors or complete arm mean/SD/n tables are supplied (pp. 73-84). Raw-score, z-score, distribution, and topic-specific displays are variants (Figures 40-41, 45-55). This entry concerns current AI assistance; session-4 essays after AI removal are recorded separately. No outcome is explicitly declared primary.

contrasts.reported: No numerical overall LLM-minus-Brain uniqueness contrast is printed. Teachers describe lower uniqueness in formulaic, apparently AI-assisted essays, with exceptions for unusual examples or quotes (p. 72). Topic results vary: LLM uniqueness is generally at or below the human mean for HAPPINESS (p. 80), while Brain-only uniqueness is below the human mean for COURAGE (p. 77). These are descriptive ratings and z-score plots, not standardized treatment effects.
Teacher uniqueness for both groups appears in group/topic displays; no numerical aggregate contrast, uncertainty, or clear overall ordering is reported.

outcomes.name: Within-group semantic similarity of essays
outcomes.question: across_people
outcomes.measure_detail: Essay embeddings from llama4:17b-scout-16e-instruct-q4_K_M are compared by pairwise cosine similarity within the current tool group (p. 57, Figure 19). PaCMAP visualizations by group, topic, and session are related descriptive variants (pp. 52-54, Figures 13-14); within-person transition distances are separate.

contrasts.reported: Text describes greater similarity in LLM essays and greater variability in Brain-only essays. Figure 19 supplies heatmaps without a printed group mean, contrast, SE, CI, or pair count. Greater raw similarity is coded as lower diversity.
Authors describe LLM essays as less variable than the other groups. Within-group heatmaps have no printed numerical contrast or uncertainty. Direction is reversed from similarity to diversity.

diversity_detail.metric: Pairwise cosine similarity; related PaCMAP cluster displays
diversity_detail.computed_over: All essay pairs within each tool group; multiple sessions and topics are represented. The paper does not state that same-writer pairs are excluded, nor clearly state whether aggregate heatmaps include session 4.
diversity_detail.uncertainty: No numerical SE, CI, or named inferential procedure for this outcome is reported in the NLP section; figures and descriptive comparisons only.
diversity_detail.notes: Greater similarity means lower diversity. Pairs are not independent people; the number of pairs is not reported. No effect size is derived.

outcomes.name: Named-entity consistency across essays: Cramer's V
outcomes.question: across_people
outcomes.measure_detail: Named entities are extracted/classified with llama4:17b-scout-16e-instruct-q4_K_M. Cramer's V summarizes association/consistency of entity distributions within each group and topic, averaged across topics (pp. 58-59, Figure 21). Entity-type frequencies in Figures 22-24 are descriptive variants, not participant counts.

contrasts.reported: Figure 21 prints * 0.02898 on the bracket connecting LLM and Brain Only. LLM has higher Cramer's V; numerical bar heights, SEs, CIs, and analysis n are not printed. Higher consistency is coded as lower diversity.
contrasts.locator: p. 59, Figure 21 (printed bracket label, visually checked); pp. 58-59, Named Entities Recognition

contrasts.reported: Figure 21 prints ** 0.00462 on the bracket connecting LLM and Search Engine. LLM has higher Cramer's V; exact arm values and uncertainty intervals are not printed.
contrasts.locator: p. 59, Figure 21 (printed bracket label, visually checked)

diversity_detail.metric: Cramer's V for named-entity distributions, averaged over topics
diversity_detail.computed_over: Named entities in essays within each group/topic; topic-level associations averaged for each group. Extraction/classification uses llama4:17b-scout-16e-instruct-q4_K_M.
diversity_detail.uncertainty: Figure 21 prints pairwise significance labels 0.02898 and 0.00462. The between-group test and independent unit are unspecified; equations (3)-(5) define the underlying chi-square/Cramer's V calculation.
diversity_detail.notes: Raw association increases with consistency, so diversity direction is reversed. Unlabeled bar heights are not exact means; entity occurrences are not independent participants.

outcomes.name: N-gram overlap and recurring vocabulary across writers
outcomes.question: across_people
outcomes.measure_detail: Frequency and overlap of lemmatized n-grams by topic and group. Method states n-gram lengths 2-5 (p. 62). Figures 25-27 show pooled/topic-specific distributions; Figures 79-86 give session variants using phrases occurring at least 3 times per essay (p. 132). That section also describes the earlier analysis as order 4 and higher, an unresolved specification inconsistency. Session-4 writing after AI removal is coded separately.

contrasts.reported: Authors describe recurring group-specific phrasing and greater homogeneity in LLM essays; Brain-only essays show distinctive phrases and a more diverse range in CHOICES. No overall overlap coefficient, uncertainty, or participant-level effect is printed.
contrasts.locator: pp. 62-65, Figures 25-27; p. 133, Figure 81; p. 143, Discussion: NLP

contrasts.reported: Both assisted groups show recurring phrases, but patterns depend on topic: LLM emphasizes career/success language in HAPPINESS whereas Search Engine uses different phrases. No single LLM-versus-search diversity contrast is printed.

diversity_detail.metric: Frequency distributions and reuse/overlap of lemmatized n-grams
diversity_detail.computed_over: Essay pools by condition and topic, plus session-specific frequency diagrams; not a per-person count of idea categories.
diversity_detail.uncertainty: No numerical SE, CI, or named inferential procedure for this outcome is reported in the NLP section; figures and descriptive comparisons only.
diversity_detail.notes: Greater overlap/repetition means lower diversity. Some n-grams come directly from prompts. No aggregate homogenization effect is supplied.

outcomes.name: Shared ontology edges across essays
outcomes.question: across_people
outcomes.measure_detail: An agent based on llama4:17b-scout-16e-instruct-q4_K_M generates each essay ontology, manually checked (p. 68). Recurrent concept edges are counted across other essays on the same topic within a group; wording is grouped by Levenshtein distance <= 10 (p. 70, Figure 37). Topic-level variant uses <= 20 (p. 71, Figure 38).

contrasts.reported: Text describes many recurring ontology edges in LLM essays, with Brain-only contributing only a handful and little intersection with the other groups. No aggregate effect, SE, CI, or test is given. Higher recurrence is coded as lower conceptual diversity.
Search Engine and LLM essays largely overlap in reused ontologies. Narrative says LLM dominates the displayed distribution, but supplies no comparable group-level diversity score or uncertainty.

diversity_detail.metric: Recurring ontology concept-pair/edge frequencies after Levenshtein matching
diversity_detail.computed_over: Each essay's edges compared with other essays on the same topic within group; additional topic-level aggregation.
diversity_detail.uncertainty: No numerical SE, CI, or named inferential procedure for this outcome is reported in the NLP section; figures and descriptive comparisons only.
diversity_detail.notes: Generating model: llama4:17b-scout-16e-instruct-q4_K_M, not an embedding model for this measure. Repeated concepts across writers, not within-writer flexibility. More recurrence means less diversity.

outcomes.name: Between-group divergence of n-gram distributions
outcomes.question: across_people
outcomes.measure_detail: Kullback-Leibler divergence compares aggregated n-gram distributions across conditions within topics and averaged across topics. Smoothing epsilon = 1e-10; normalized within topic (pp. 57-58, Figure 20). This is between-group separation, not a within-group diversity level for each arm.

contrasts.reported: Brain-only and LLM distributions diverge for ART, CHOICES, COURAGE, FORETHOUGHT, and PHILANTHROPY; LOYALTY and HAPPINESS show less difference. Heatmaps have no printed cell values or inferential statistics and do not establish which arm has higher within-arm diversity.
Separation varies by topic; Search Engine diverges from LLM and Brain-only particularly in LOYALTY and HAPPINESS. No numerical arm contrast or uncertainty is printed.

diversity_detail.metric: Normalized Kullback-Leibler divergence of group-level n-gram distributions
diversity_detail.computed_over: Ordered pairs of condition-level n-gram distributions within topics, plus an average across topics.
diversity_detail.uncertainty: No numerical SE, CI, or named inferential procedure for this outcome is reported in the NLP section; figures and descriptive comparisons only.
diversity_detail.notes: Between-distribution distance is not an estimate of a reduction in within-condition diversity. No sign reversal or effect-size calculation is applied; direction reflects mixed topic patterns.

outcomes.name: Essay uniqueness after AI removal: English-teacher ratings
outcomes.question: after_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Two English teachers, blinded to group assignments and study motivations, scored essays on a 0-5 scale (p. 72). Figures report averaged essay assessments and aggregations by topic, session, and group; no participant-level standard errors or complete arm mean/SD/n tables are supplied (pp. 73-84). LLM-to-Brain essays in session 4 were written without AI on a previously chosen topic (pp. 28, 117). Topic-specific z-score plots and discussion address uniqueness after removal. There is no concurrent never-AI fourth-session arm.
outcomes.delay: Session 4 follows three earlier sessions; the interval in days is not stated (pp. 23, 28, 117). The four-month study duration is not a participant-level follow-up interval.

contrasts.reported: Page 122 describes low teacher uniqueness in FORETHOUGHT and PERFECT after AI removal, citing Figures 51 and 54. However, p. 76 says session 4 is highly scored in most cases, and topic plots contain both high and low session-4 scores. No numerical aggregate uniqueness difference or uncertainty is printed; the comparison is with earlier Brain-only writing, not a contemporaneous randomized contrast.
contrasts.locator: p. 76, Scoring per topic; p. 80, Figure 51; p. 83, Figure 54; p. 122, Cognitive processing

outcomes.name: Recurring vocabulary and narrower ideas after AI removal
outcomes.question: after_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Session-specific n-gram diagrams compare LLM-to-Brain essays with earlier tool-group essays on the same topics (pp. 132-136, Figures 79-86). Phrases occurring at least 3 times per essay are displayed. Shared/reused phrases are interpreted as lingering LLM influence; this is a corpus-level pattern, with no independent per-person diversity estimate.
outcomes.delay: Session 4 follows three earlier sessions; the interval in days is not stated (pp. 23, 28, 117). The four-month study duration is not a participant-level follow-up interval.

contrasts.reported: Authors report that LLM-to-Brain participants reused vocabulary and structure from earlier LLM writing, unlike original Brain-only writing. COURAGE, FORETHOUGHT, and PERFECT are highlighted as narrower/repetitive; CHOICES shows a more diverse range. No aggregate effect or uncertainty is printed, and authors call the conclusion preliminary.
contrasts.locator: pp. 133-136, Figures 81-86; p. 151, discussion preceding Limitations

diversity_detail.computed_over: Essay pools within topic and current tool group across sessions; session-4 no-tool essays from former LLM users compared descriptively with earlier LLM and Brain-only essays.
diversity_detail.uncertainty: No numerical SE, CI, or named inferential procedure for this outcome is reported in the NLP section; figures and descriptive comparisons only.
diversity_detail.notes: Coded after_ai because scored session-4 output was produced without AI. Lower diversity describes the authors' overall interpretation, with topic variation and only a returning subset. Comparison is across sessions/tool histories, not an independently randomized follow-up.

outcomes.name: Within-person semantic change after AI removal: PaCMAP distance
outcomes.question: after_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Normalized PaCMAP distance between a participant's session-4 essay and earlier same-topic essays, averaged per participant and topic (pp. 52-53, Figure 12). Embeddings are described as llama4:17b-scout-16e-instruct-q4_K_M (p. 53). This is within-writer change, not between-writer diversity or a validated creativity score.
outcomes.delay: Session 4 follows three earlier sessions; the interval in days is not stated (pp. 23, 28, 117). The four-month study duration is not a participant-level follow-up interval.

contrasts.control_arm: Earlier LLM essay by the same returning participant
contrasts.reported: Figure 12 displays a large normalized LLM-to-Brain distance, but no numerical bar label, SE, CI, or test statistic. A distance between essays does not determine whether later creativity is higher or lower. The figure also displays Search Engine transitions absent from the session-4 protocol; interpretation needs clarification.
contrasts.locator: pp. 52-53, Figure 12; pp. 28 and 117, session-4 protocol

outcomes.name: Essay uniqueness: AI-judge ratings with AI available
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Multi-step agentic judge based on llama4:17b-scout-16e-instruct-q4_K_M rates the same criteria as teachers, using a writing-expert system prompt and refinement loop (pp. 71-73, Figure 39). Raw, z-score, distribution, and topic-specific displays are variants (Figures 40-55). AI-versus-teacher scoring agreement is not the experimental treatment comparison.

contrasts.reported: AI-judge uniqueness is shown by group, session, and topic, but no aggregate LLM-minus-Brain contrast or uncertainty is printed. Topic narratives describe high AI uniqueness for LLM writing in LOYALTY and disagreement with teachers; ART has low AI uniqueness despite high teacher scores.
AI-judge uniqueness for both groups is displayed, but no aggregate numerical treatment contrast or clear overall ordering is stated.

outcomes.name: Essay content quality: English-teacher ratings
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Two English teachers, blinded to group assignments and study motivations, scored essays on a 0-5 scale (p. 72). Figures report averaged essay assessments and aggregations by topic, session, and group; no participant-level standard errors or complete arm mean/SD/n tables are supplied (pp. 73-84). Content is output quality. Figure 42 and topic-specific z-score plots are variants. AI-judge content is reported but omitted as a separate outcome under the 15-outcome cap.

Teachers also describe formulaic apparently AI-assisted essays receiving low content scores. No overall numerical LLM-minus-Brain content effect or uncertainty is printed.
contrasts.locator: p. 72, teacher explanation; pp. 73-74, Figures 41-42; p. 77, Figure 48

contrasts.reported: Both groups' content assessments are displayed; no aggregate numerical LLM-versus-search contrast or clear overall ordering is reported.

outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Two English teachers, blinded to group assignments and study motivations, scored essays on a 0-5 scale (p. 72). Figures report averaged essay assessments and aggregations by topic, session, and group; no participant-level standard errors or complete arm mean/SD/n tables are supplied (pp. 73-84). Structural quality of the written essay. Figure 43 and topic-specific z-score plots are variants. Automated counterpart is noted but not separately retained under the outcome cap.

Group/topic structure and organization ratings are plotted, without an overall numerical contrast or clear LLM-versus-Search ordering.

outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Two English teachers, blinded to group assignments and study motivations, scored essays on a 0-5 scale (p. 72). Figures report averaged essay assessments and aggregations by topic, session, and group; no participant-level standard errors or complete arm mean/SD/n tables are supplied (pp. 73-84). outcomes.name: Essay length: word and sentence counts
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Figure 16 prints group averages for words and sentences. Sentence count is a companion operationalization of length, not idea fluency. No SD, SE, CI, or essay count accompanies the means; inclusion of session 4 in the aggregate is unspecified.

contrasts.reported: Average Words: LLM 373.2; Brain Only 373.3. Average Sentences: LLM 19.0; Brain Only 17.2. Labels printed in Figure 16. Word means are very similar while LLM sentence count is higher; no inferential comparison is supplied.
Average Words: LLM 373.2; Search Engine 318.7. Average Sentences: LLM 19.0; Search Engine 15.6. No SD, SE, CI, or inferential contrast is supplied.

outcomes.measure_detail: Cosine distance from participant essays to a standard essay generated by llama4:17b-scout-16e-instruct-q4_K_M from the same assignment, averaged across topics (pp. 55-56, Figures 17-18). Output-level benchmark distance, not within-condition diversity; the study still assigns people to AI assistance.

contrasts.reported: Average cosine distance: LLM 0.48301; Brain Only 0.48579. Text describes these as about the same. No SD, SE, CI, or test statistic is given.
contrasts.locator: p. 56, Figure 18 (printed labels, visually checked at enlarged scale)

sample_overlap.shares_participants_with: No other paper is identified as sharing this sample. The fourth session reuses a subset of the same experiment; it is not an independent sample.
sample_overlap.quote: we only present results for these 18 participants who took part in all 4 sessions.

company_involvement.description: The conflict-of-interest statement says Nataliya Kosmyna held a Visiting Researcher position at Google at publication, but all project work was completed before that affiliation. Other authors declare no conflicts and the study reports no external funding; no corporate role in conducting the experiment is stated.
company_involvement.locator: p. 154, Conflict of Interest and Funding

eligibility.reason: Methods explicitly state random assignment of people to ChatGPT, search, or no aid (p. 23), and 54 people are analyzed across the original arms (p. 22; p. 3, Table 1). Essays receive blinded teacher uniqueness ratings (p. 72) and computed cross-writer similarity/overlap measures (pp. 57-71). The qualifying design is the initial laboratory RCT, not AI-versus-human generation or the optional follow-up alone. Session 4 uses only 18 returning participants, has no new randomization or concurrent never-AI arm, and cannot independently meet the size criterion (pp. 45-46, 117).

one_line_finding: Among 54 analyzed writers (p. 22), ChatGPT essays showed greater named-entity consistency than unaided essays (Figure 21, p. 59: p = 0.02898), while teacher uniqueness ratings were topic-dependent and lacked an overall numerical treatment effect (pp. 72-84).
open_questions: Which exact revision is the saved preprint? No printed arXiv version; June 2025 publication statements coexist with a reference retrieved December 12, 2025 (pp. 151, 154, 166).

What were the numbers randomized and lost in each arm? The methods give recruited/completed/analyzed counts, not an assignment-stage denominator; educational-status subtotals do not reconcile with 54 (p. 22).
Which ChatGPT model/version was supplied to participants? Intervention methods do not name it (pp. 23, 27).
Do pooled group figures include session 4, and how are original versus current tool groups distinguished? Aggregates may mix randomized first-phase essays with crossover-subset essays (pp. 52-84).

Figure 12 and its prose include Search Engine transitions in session 4, although Table 1 says there was no Search Engine session 4 and the protocol describes only LLM/Brain switching (pp. 4, 28, 52-53, 117).

How were NLP significance tests obtained, particularly the Cramer's V comparisons in Figure 21? Independent units and test procedure are unspecified; participant-level uncertainty cannot be recovered from printed results (pp. 58-59).

Prose and Figure 15 inconsistently describe word length versus essay word counts/variability; Figure 16 shows nearly equal LLM and Brain-only word means despite the shorter-Brain-only description in Table 1 (pp. 4, 55).

Session-4 interpretations need reconciliation: reassigned group labels for quotation performance in pp. 46-47 conflict with the original-group interpretation on p. 150; p. 76 describes generally high session-4 scores while p. 122 emphasizes low uniqueness for selected topics. Memory outcomes are not coded as creative-output outcomes.

Are participant-linked essay scores, repeated-measure identifiers, exact semantic-similarity summaries, and code available? The PDF gives a project-information website (p. 5), no explicit data/code repository, and EEG appendices rather than missing essay-outcome uncertainty.
notes: Screened on 2026-10-09. The entire markdown, including references and Appendices A-BC, was read in contiguous chunks; relevant text, counts, and numerical chart labels were checked against the PDF. Locators use PDF page numbers. One longitudinal experiment is coded: session 4 is a returning subset, not another study or 18 additional people. A procedural pilot with three participants is mentioned on p. 23 but has no reported creative-output results and is not counted as another analyzed study. No effects, SDs, SEs, or graphic bar heights were calculated. The paper does not explicitly designate a primary creativity/diversity outcome. More than 15 potentially relevant measure/timing combinations exist; the main 15 are retained under form rule 7. Output measures omitted as separate rows: ambiguous word/essay-length variability (p. 55, Figure 15; printed per-group p-value labels: LLM 0.39, Search Engine 0.02, Brain Only 0.49, tested null unspecified); teacher and AI Accuracy; AI content, language/style, structure/organization; Length ratings named in the rubric but not distinctly summarized in displayed scoring labels (pp. 72-84); automated uniqueness and other quality metrics on session-4 no-AI essays; and separate session-4 Brain-to-LLM rating/transition variants. Topic-specific versions and raw/z-score visualizations of retained outcomes are grouped. Named-entity type frequencies accompany Cramer's V; between-writer PaCMAP clusters accompany cosine similarity. The non-output inventory comprises quotation ability/correctness, prompt recognition/recall, reported ownership, satisfaction/preference and writing strategies (pp. 30-51); prior ChatGPT use and prompt classifications (pp. 65-68); interview clusters (p. 85, Appendix A); EEG dDTF by frequency band, electrode pair, group, session, topic (pp. 86-142, Appendices B-BC); and estimated energy consumption (p. 152, Table 4). These are excluded from creative-output outcomes. Google Ads/N-gram/Trends illustrations are contextual, not independent participant studies (pp. 143-145, Figures 90-92). Diversity direction is reversed for similarity, association, or repeated concepts; between-group KL divergence and within-writer change cannot alone establish a higher/lower creative effect. Exact output counts are not supplied for retained analyses, so n_units remains null; repeated essays, entities, phrases, and pairs are not independent participants. Data/code URL fields remain empty because the PDF does not state repository URLs.
